claim: The Longshanks selection experiment selected mice over 20 generations for longer tibiae relative to body mass, resulting in 13% longer tibiae in two replicates.
source: Here we present a genomic dissection of the Longshanks selection experiment, in which mice were selectively bred over 20 generations for longer tibiae relative to body mass, resulting in 13% longer tibiae in two replicates.
evidence: The abstract directly states the experimental design and outcome with specific quantitative results.

claim: The selection response in the Longshanks experiment involved both polygenic adaptation and discrete loci of major effect.
source: We synthesized evolutionary theory, genome sequences and molecular genetics to understand the selection response and found that it involved both polygenic adaptation and discrete loci of major effect, with the strongest loci tending to be selected in parallel between replicates.
evidence: The abstract presents findings from the genomic analysis showing mixed genetic architecture.

claim: The strongest loci tended to be selected in parallel between replicates.
source: We synthesized evolutionary theory, genome sequences and molecular genetics to understand the selection response and found that it involved both polygenic adaptation and discrete loci of major effect, with the strongest loci tending to be selected in parallel between replicates.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the analysis.

claim: Selection may favor de-repression of bone growth through inactivating two limb enhancers of Nkx3-2.
source: We show that selection may favor de-repression of bone growth through inactivating two limb enhancers of an inhibitor, Nkx3-2.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from molecular genetic analysis.

claim: It is possible to connect individual base-pair changes to the overall selection response.
source: Our integrative genomic analyses thus show that it is possible to connect individual base-pair changes to the overall selection response.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this statement based on the study's findings.

claim: Beneficial alleles in mammals typically come from standing genetic variation rather than new mutations.
source: Because beneficial alleles in mammals typically come from standing genetic variation rather than new mutations like in microbes, this loss of diversity would ultimately impose a limit on the ability of small populations to adapt.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Mammals respond readily to selection in many traits, both in nature and in the laboratory.
source: Nonetheless, mammals respond readily to selection in many traits, both in nature and in the laboratory (Darwin, 1859; Gingerich, 2001; Garland and Rose, 2009; Keightley et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The infinitesimal model has performed remarkably well across a wide range of selection experiments.
source: Broadly speaking, the infinitesimal model has performed remarkably well across a wide range of selection experiments, and the model is the basis for commercial breeding (Walsh and Lynch, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Walsh and Lynch, 2018.

claim: The mammalian limb is an ideal model to study the dynamics of complex traits under selection.
source: The mammalian limb is an ideal model to study the dynamics of complex traits under selection: it is both morphologically complex and functionally diverse, reflecting its adaptive value; and limb development has been studied extensively in mammals, birds and fishes as a genetic and evolutionary paradigm (Petit et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by reasoning and a citation.

claim: Three base populations were established with 14 pairs each by sampling from Hsd:ICR commercial mouse stock.
source: At the start of the Longshanks experiment, we established three base populations with 14 pairs each by sampling from a genetically diverse, commercial mouse stock (Hsd:ICR, also known as CD-1; derived from mixed breeding of classical laboratory mice [Yalcin et al., 2010]).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup with specific details.

claim: In LS1 and LS2, breeders were selected for the longest tibia relative to the cube root of body mass, corresponding to 15–20% of all offspring.
source: In two replicate 'Longshanks' lines (LS1 and LS2), we bred mice by pairing 16 males and females (and excluding sibling pairs) with the longest tibia relative to the cube root of body mass for each sex. This corresponds to 15–20% of all offspring (only details essential to understanding our analysis are summarized here. See Marchini et al., 2014 for a detailed description of the breeding scheme).
evidence: This describes the selection protocol with specific quantitative details.

claim: LS1 and LS2 showed a strong and significant response to selection in tibia length of 0.29 and 0.26 Haldane per generation.
source: In LS1 and LS2, we observed a strong and significant response to selection in tibia length (0.29 and 0.26 Haldane or standard deviations (s.d.) per generation, from a selection differential of 0.73 s.d. in LS1 and 0.62 s.d. in LS2).
evidence: This presents quantitative results from the selection experiment.

claim: Over 20 generations, selection produced increases of 5.27 and 4.81 s.d. in LS1 and LS2, respectively.
source: Over 20 generations, selection for longer relative tibia length produced increases of 5.27 and 4.81 s.d. in LS1 and LS2, respectively (or 12.7% and 13.1% in tibia length), with a modest decrease in body mass (−1.5% in LS1 and −3.7% in LS2; Student's t-test, p<2 × 10−4 and p<1 × 10−8, respectively; Figure 1B and C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; n.b. this relationship was in part biased by the F1 generation, which were fed a different diet and phenotyped three weeks later than later generations, see Marchini et al., 2014 for details).
evidence: This presents quantitative results with statistical tests and references to figures.

claim: The Control line showed no directional change in tibia length or body mass.
source: By contrast, Ctrl showed no directional change in tibia length or body mass (Figure 1C; Student's t-test, p>0.05).
evidence: This presents a negative result with statistical test and figure reference.

claim: The approximately 5 s.d. change in 20 generations is rapid compared to typical rates observed in nature.
source: This approximately 5 s.d. change in 20 generations is rapid compared to typical rates observed in nature (Hendry and Kinnison, 1999, but see Grant and Grant, 2002) but is in line with responses seen in selection experiments (Gingerich, 2001; Keightley et al., 2001; Falconer and Mackay, 1996; Pitchers et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim compares the observed rate to literature values with multiple citations.

claim: The simulation framework faithfully recapitulates the artificial selection experiment by integrating trait measurements, selection regime, pedigree and genetic diversity.
source: We therefore developed a simulation that faithfully recapitulates the artificial selection experiment by integrating the trait measurements, selection regime, pedigree and genetic diversity of the Longshanks selection experiment, in order to generate an accurate expectation for the genomic response.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology developed for the study.

claim: The predicted increase in inbreeding closely matched the observed data.
source: Results from simulations seeded with actual genotypes or haplotypes showed that overall, the predicted increase in inbreeding closely matched the observed data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This compares simulation results to observed data.

claim: Allele frequency shifts exceeding the infinitesimal model threshold would suggest that discrete loci contribute significantly to the selection response.
source: Because our simulations assume infinitesimal effects of loci, allele frequency shifts exceeding this stringent threshold would suggest that discrete loci contribute significantly to the selection response.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the simulation framework.

claim: All individuals of the founder (F0) and 17th generation (F17) were sequenced to an average of 2.91-fold coverage.
source: To detect the genomic changes in the actual Longshanks experiment, we sequenced all individuals of the founder (F0) and 17th generation (F17) to an average of 2.91-fold coverage (range: 0.73–20.6×; n = 169 with <10% missing F0 individuals; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the sequencing methodology with specific coverage values.

claim: Across the three lines, an average of 6.7 million segregating SNPs were found.
source: Across the three lines, we found similar levels of diversity, with an average of 6.7 million (M) segregating SNPs (approximately 0.025%, or 1 SNP per four kbp; Supplementary file 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This presents quantitative results from sequencing analysis.

claim: The founder populations showed negligible divergence with across-line FST on the order of 1 × 10−4.
source: We checked the founder populations to confirm negligible divergence between the three founder populations (across-line FST on the order of 1 × 10−4), which increased to 0.18 at F17 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This presents population genetic statistics from the data.

claim: By F17, the number of segregating SNPs dropped to around 5.8 M.
source: By F17, the number of segregating SNPs dropped to around 5.8 M (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This presents a quantitative result from sequencing analysis.

claim: The 13% drop in diversity (0.9M SNPs genome-wide) is predicted by drift.
source: This 13% drop in diversity (0.9M SNPs genome-wide) is predicted by drift.
evidence: This interprets the observed data in light of population genetic theory.

claim: Simulations confirmed that selection contributed negligibly to the drop in diversity.
source: Our simulations confirmed this and moreover, showed that selection contributed negligibly to the drop in diversity (Appendix, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D).
evidence: This presents results from simulations.

claim: 169 windows belonging to eight clusters showed significant shifts in allele frequency in LS1 and/or LS2.
source: We averaged ∆z2 within 10 kbp windows (see Methods for details), and found 169 windows belonging to eight clusters (i.e., loci) that had significant shifts in allele frequency in LS1 and/or LS2 (corresponding to 9 and 164 clustered windows respectively at p≤0.05 under HINF, max LD; ∆z2 ≥0.33 π2; genome-wide ∆z2 = 0.02 ± 0.03 π2; Figure 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3; see Methods for details) and 8 windows in three clusters in Ctrl (genome-wide ∆z2 = 0.01 ± 0.02 π2).
evidence: This presents quantitative results from the genomic analysis with statistical thresholds.

claim: The eight loci in Longshanks each overlapped between 2 to 179 genes and together contained 11 candidate genes with known roles in bone, cartilage and/or limb development.
source: The eight loci in Longshanks each overlapped between 2 to 179 genes and together contained 11 candidate genes with known roles in bone, cartilage and/or limb development (e.g., Nkx3-2 and Sox9; Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This presents results from gene annotation analysis.

claim: Four out of the eight loci contain genes with a 'short tibia' or 'short limb' knockout phenotype.
source: Four out of the eight loci contain genes with a 'short tibia' or 'short limb' knockout phenotype (Table 1; p≤0.032 from 1000 permutations, see Methods for details).
evidence: This presents results from enrichment analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Only fibrillin 2 (Fbn2) is polymorphic for SNPs coding for different amino acids among genes at these loci with limb knockout phenotypes.
source: Of the broader set of genes at these loci with any limb knockout phenotypes, only fibrillin 2 (Fbn2) is polymorphic for SNPs coding for different amino acids, suggesting that for the majority of loci with large shifts in allele frequency, gene regulation was likely important in the selection response (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Supplementary file 3; see Appendix for further analyses on enrichment in gene functions, protein-coding vs. cis-acting changes and clustering with loci affecting human height).
evidence: This presents results from coding variant analysis and draws an inference.

claim: The ∆z2 profiles of LS1 and LS2 were more similar to each other than to Ctrl.
source: Indeed, the ∆z2 profiles of LS1 and LS2 were more similar to each other than to Ctrl (Figure 2 and 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Pearson's correlation in ∆z2 from 10 kbp windows: LS1–LS2: 0.21 vs. LS1–Ctrl: 0.06 and LS2–Ctrl: 0.05).
evidence: This presents quantitative correlation analysis results.

claim: Six out of eight significant loci at the HINF, max LD threshold were line-specific.
source: Six out of eight significant loci at the HINF, max LD threshold were line-specific, even though all eight selected alleles were present in the F0 generation in both lines.
evidence: This presents results from the parallelism analysis.

claim: The two parallel loci ranked first and second by selection coefficient, both with s > 0.3.
source: However, the two remaining loci that ranked first and second by selection coefficient were parallel, both with s > 0.3 (Figure 3B; note that as outliers, the selection coefficient may be substantially overestimated, but their rank order should remain the same), supporting the idea that the probability of parallelism can be high among those loci with the greatest selection advantage (Orr, 2005).
evidence: This presents quantitative results and cites supporting theory.

claim: The signature of parallelism was significantly enriched in the comparison between the selected replicates.
source: In contrast to the subtle differences within each line in changes in global diversity over 17 generations (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), we found the signature of parallelism to be significantly enriched in the comparison between the selected replicates (χ2 test, LS1–LS2: p≤1 × 10−10), as opposed to comparisons between each selected line and Ctrl (LS1–Ctrl: p>0.01 and LS2–Ctrl: p>0.2, both non-significant after correcting for multiple testing), or between simulated replicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; see Appendix for details).
evidence: This presents statistical test results comparing parallelism across different comparisons.

claim: The locus on chromosome 5 at 41–42 Mbp showed the strongest estimated selection coefficient.
source: Between the two major parallel loci, we chose the locus on chromosome 5 (Chr5) at 41–42 Mbp for functional validation because it showed the strongest estimated selection coefficient, its signature of selection was clear, and crucially for functional characterization, it contains only three genes, including Nkx3-2 (also known as Bapx1), a known regulator of bone maturation (Figure 2 and 4A) (Provot et al., 2006).
evidence: This explains the rationale for selecting this locus for functional validation with citation.

claim: The pattern of variation at the Chr5 locus resembles a selective sweep spanning 1 Mbp.
source: At this locus, the pattern of variation resembles a selective sweep spanning 1 Mbp (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the observed pattern in the data.

claim: No recombinant was found in the entire 1 Mbp region between F0 and F17 individuals.
source: Comparison between F0 and F17 individuals revealed no recombinant in this entire region (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, top panel), precluding fine-mapping using recombinants.
evidence: This presents a negative result from the data analysis.

claim: No coding changes existed for either Rab28 or Nkx3-2 within the topologically associating domain.
source: First, we determined that no coding changes existed for either Rab28 or Nkx3-2, the two genes located within the topologically associating domain (TAD, which mark chromosome segments with shared gene regulatory logic) (Dixon et al., 2012).
evidence: This presents a negative result from sequence analysis with citation.

claim: Nkx3-2 and Rab28 showed robust expression in the developing fore- and hind limb buds at E12.5.
source: We then performed in situ hybridization and detected robust expression of Nkx3-2 and Rab28 in the developing fore- and hind limb buds of Ctrl, LS1 and LS2 E12.5, in a domain broadly overlapping the presumptive zeugopod, the region including the tibia (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This presents results from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Bod1l showed only weak or undetectable expression in the developing limb bud.
source: Consistent with this, Bod1l showed only weak or undetectable expression in the developing limb bud (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This presents results from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Three novel enhancer candidates (N1, N2 and N3) were identified carrying three, one and three SNPs respectively.
source: Here we found three novel enhancer candidates (N1, N2 and N3) carrying three, one and three SNPs respectively, all of which showed significant allele frequency shifts in LS1 and LS2 (Figure 4B and C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This presents results from chromatin profiling and variant analysis.

claim: The N1 and N3 sequences formed long-range looping contacts with the Nkx3-2 promoter.
source: Chromosome conformation capture assays showed that the N1 and N3 sequences formed long-range looping contacts with the Nkx3-2 promoter—a hallmark of enhancers—despite as much as 600 kbp of intervening sequence (Figure 4B).
evidence: This presents results from 4C-Seq experiments.

claim: The F0 alleles of the N1 and N3 enhancers drove robust and consistent lacZ expression in the developing limb buds at E12.5.
source: We found that the F0 alleles of the N1 and N3 enhancers (three SNPs each in about one kbp) drove robust and consistent lacZ expression in the developing limb buds (N1 and N3) as well as in expanded trunk domains (N3) at E12.5 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This presents results from transgenic reporter assays.

claim: The F17 alleles of the N1 and N3 enhancers drove consistently weak, nearly undetectable lacZ expression.
source: In contrast, transgenic reporters carrying the selected F17 alleles of the N1 and N3 enhancers drove consistently weak, nearly undetectable lacZ expression (Figure 4E).
evidence: This presents results from transgenic reporter assays.

claim: Switching from the F0 to the F17 enhancer alleles led to a nearly complete loss in activity at developmental stage E12.5.
source: Thus, switching from the F0 to the F17 enhancer alleles led to a nearly complete loss in activity ('loss-of-function') at developmental stage E12.5.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transgenic reporter assay results.

claim: The loss-of-function at the Nkx3-2 enhancers is consistent with the role of Nkx3-2 as a repressor in long bone maturation.
source: This is consistent with the role of Nkx3-2 as a repressor in long bone maturation (Provot et al., 2006).
evidence: This connects the experimental results to known biology with a citation.

claim: The selected allele steadily increased from around 0.17 to 0.85 in LS1 and 0.98 in LS2 but fluctuated around 0.25 in Ctrl.
source: The selected allele steadily increased from around 0.17 to 0.85 in LS1 and 0.98 in LS2 but fluctuated around 0.25 in Ctrl (Figure 5B).
evidence: This presents results from targeted genotyping across all generations.

claim: A change of around 0.7 in allele frequency would correspond to a selection coefficient s of ~0.24 ± 0.12 at the Nkx3-2 locus.
source: We estimated that such a change of around 0.7 in allele frequency would correspond to a selection coefficient s of ~0.24 ± 0.12 at this locus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; see Appendix section on 'Estimating selection coefficient of the top-ranking locus, Nkx3-2, from changes in allele frequency').
evidence: This presents an estimated parameter value from population genetic analysis.

claim: The Nkx3-2 locus would contribute 9.4% of the total selection response (limits 3.6–15.5%).
source: By extending our simulation framework to allow for a major locus against an infinitesimal background, we find that the Nkx3-2 locus would contribute 9.4% of the total selection response (limits 3.6–15.5%; see Appendix section 'Estimating selection coefficient' for details) in order to produce a shift of 0.7 in allele frequency over 17 generations.
evidence: This presents results from simulation analysis.

claim: Each selected allele at the Nkx3-2 locus increases tibia length by 0.36% (95% conf. int.: 0.07–0.64%, p=0.0171).
source: Using this alternative approach, we estimated that each selected allele increases tibia length by 0.36% (N = 1569, 95% conf. int.: 0.07–0.64%, p=0.0171).
evidence: This presents results from a linear mixed animal model analysis with statistical significance.

claim: The Nkx3-2 locus alone would account for approximately 4% of the overall 12.9% increase in tibia length.
source: Multiplying the effect with the increase in the allele frequency suggests that the Nkx3-2 locus alone would account for approximately 4% of the overall 12.9% increase in tibia length.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the animal model results.

claim: Selection response can be steady and robust even in extremely bottlenecked populations.
source: An important conclusion from the Longshanks experiment is that selection response can be steady and robust even in extremely bottlenecked populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall experimental results.

claim: Tibia length increased readily and repeatedly in response to selection even with as few as 14–16 breeding pairs per generation.
source: That is, we found that tibia length increased readily and repeatedly in response to selection even with as few as 14–16 breeding pairs per generation.
evidence: This summarizes the experimental design and outcome.

claim: Generation 17 was still only a fraction of the way to the expected limit for the selection response at ~2Ne generations.
source: The sustained response was possible because the lines were founded with enough standing variation, and generation 17 was still only a fraction of the way to the expected limit for the selection response at ~2Ne generations (Robertson, 1960), estimated here to be around 90 (see legend for Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Appendix on 'Estimating the selection coefficient').
evidence: This interprets the results in light of quantitative genetic theory with citation.

claim: The estimated Ne of 46 in the Longshanks experiment is comparable to those in natural populations like the Soay sheep, Darwin's finches or Tasmanian devils.
source: The estimated Ne of 46 in the Longshanks experiment, while small, is comparable to those in natural populations like the Soay sheep (McRae et al., 2005), Darwin's finches (Grant and Grant, 1992) or Tasmanian devils (Epstein et al., 2016) (this last study documents a rapid and parallel evolutionary response to transmissible tumors).
evidence: This compares the experimental parameter to natural populations with citations.

claim: For a short bout of selection, selection response depends overwhelmingly on standing genetic variation, with little to no contribution from de novo mutations.
source: Accordingly, we also expect very different dynamics during short- vs. long-term selection response: for a short bout of selection, such as the 20 generations analyzed in this study, selection response depends overwhelmingly on standing genetic variation, with little to no contribution from de novo mutations (Hill, 1982; Weber and Diggins, 1990).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation supported by citations.

claim: Over the long term, de novo mutations would contribute increasingly to selection response.
source: Over the long term, however, de novo mutations would contribute increasingly to selection response.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation about long-term evolution.

claim: There has long been broad empirical support for adaptation from standing genetic variation in nature and breeding.
source: There has long been broad empirical support for adaptation from standing genetic variation in nature (Jones et al., 2012; Epstein et al., 2016; Hancock et al., 2011) and breeding (Sheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: The infinitesimal model is still the most predictive model by far in practical quantitative genetics for diverse domesticated species.
source: To put our finding of a mixed genetic architecture into perspective, it is worth noting that the infinitesimal model is still the most predictive model by far in practical quantitative genetics, for diverse domesticated species from cattle to crops, despite its intrinsically unrealistic assumptions (Hill et al., 2008; Lynch and Walsh, 1998; Hill and Zhang, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the field supported by citations.

claim: Current genomic data for many traits is consistent with a very large number of loci, each with a small effect.
source: In general, current genomic data for many traits is consistent with a very large number of loci, each with a small effect.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of genomic knowledge.

claim: Height in humans shows high heritability and a highly dispersed genetic architecture with the top-ranked locus accounting for only 0.8% of the variation explained.
source: Height in humans is often cited as the classical complex trait under possible selection of unknown (and much debated) intensity (see Turchin et al., 2012; Berg and Coop, 2014; Barton et al., 2019). It shows high heritability and a highly dispersed genetic architecture (with the top-ranked locus accounting for only 0.8% of the variation explained in cosmopolitan European populations) (Weedon et al., 2007; Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about human genetics supported by multiple citations.

claim: As few as 4 to 6 loci account for 83% and 50% of the variation in height in horses and dogs, respectively.
source: In contrast, as few as 4 to 6 loci account for 83% and 50% of the variation in height in horses and dogs, respectively (Makvandi-Nejad et al., 2012; Rimbault et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about animal genetics supported by citations.

claim: The major allele at the IGF1 locus in dogs stems from a standing genetic variant.
source: Interestingly, and in line with our experiment, the major allele at the IGF1 locus stems from a standing genetic variant, despite many factors that may theoretically favor large-effect de novo mutations (Sutter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about dog genetics supported by a citation.

claim: Parallel evolution is often seen as a hallmark for detecting selection.
source: Parallel evolution is often seen as a hallmark for detecting selection (Chan et al., 2012; Schluter et al., 2004; Chan et al., 2010; Martin and Orgogozo, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about evolutionary biology supported by citations.

claim: Little parallelism was observed between selected lines and Ctrl, or between simulated replicates under selection.
source: However, we observed little parallelism between selected lines and Ctrl, or between simulated replicates under selection, even though the simulated haplotypes were sampled directly from actual founders.
evidence: This presents results from the parallelism analysis.

claim: Parallelism depends on both shared selection pressure and the availability of large-effect loci that confer a substantial selection advantage.
source: This underscores that parallelism depends on both shared selection pressure (absent in Ctrl) and the availability of large-effect loci that confer a substantial selection advantage (absent under the infinitesimal model; Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the parallelism analysis results.

claim: The originally common F0 variant of the N1 enhancer shows deep functional conservation and can recapitulate fin nkx3.2 expression in fishes.
source: Through in-depth dissection of the Nkx3-2 locus, our data show in fine detail how the selective value of standing variants depends strongly on the selection regime: the originally common F0 variant of the N1 enhancer shows deep functional conservation and can evidently recapitulate fin nkx3.2 expression in fishes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This presents results from transgenic assays in stickleback fish.

claim: In the Longshanks experiment selection strongly favored the weaker allele at the N1 enhancer.
source: Yet, in the Longshanks experiment selection strongly favored the weaker allele (Figure 5B).
evidence: This presents results from the allele frequency trajectory analysis.

claim: Both gain-of-function (Gli3) and loss-of-function (Nkx3-2) variants could be favored by selection.
source: In fact, our molecular dissection of two loci show that both gain-of-function (Gli3) and loss-of-function (Nkx3-2) variants could be favored by selection (Figure 4E and 5A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This summarizes results from functional validation of two loci.

claim: Loss of NKX3-2 function in human SMMD patients manifests in opposite ways in different bone types as short trunk and long limbs.
source: To our surprise, the same loss of NKX3-2 function in human SMMD patients manifests in opposite ways in different bone types as short trunk and long limbs (Hellemans et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about human genetics supported by a citation.

claim: The expression domains of the N1 (limb) and N3 (limb and trunk) enhancers match the affected bones in SMMD patients.
source: This matches the expression domains of our N1 (limb) and N3 (limb and trunk) enhancers (Figure 5A).
evidence: This connects the experimental results to human disease phenotypes.

claim: The F17 haplotype was doubly beneficial at both enhancers for the limb and potentially also trunk target tissues under the novel selection regime.
source: Evidently, in the absence of lethal coding mutations, the F17 haplotype was doubly beneficial at both enhancers for the limb and potentially also trunk target tissues under the novel selection regime in the Longshanks selection experiment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the functional validation results and human disease data.

claim: The Nkx3-2 locus contributes ~10% of the overall selection response.
source: We estimate that these enhancer variants, along with any other tightly linked beneficial SNPs, segregate as a single locus, which in turn contributes ~10% of the overall selection response.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate from simulation and animal model analyses.

claim: It is possible to identify some of the individual SNPs that have contributed to the response to selection on morphology.
source: Using the Longshanks selection experiment and synthesizing theory, empirical data and molecular genetics, we show that it is possible to identify some of the individual SNPs that have contributed to the response to selection on morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall study.

claim: Discrete, large-effect loci are revealed by their parallel response.
source: In particular, discrete, large-effect loci are revealed by their parallel response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the parallelism analysis.
